title: The du'a of Ta'if
hookLine: in an orchard outside Ta'if he prays: to You I complain of my weakness; if You are not angry with me, I don't mind (sirah)
carry: if you're not angry, I don't mind

lines: IN THE SHADE OF A VINE.
cards: The crowd has fallen back. He's sitting in the shade of a vine, against the wall of an orchard that belongs to two men of Quraysh. Refused by three leaders, jeered at by a town, he has nowhere obvious to go next.
What would anyone say, alone, in a moment like that? A complaint about the people of Ta'if would make sense. So would a plea to be avenged.
Ibn Ishaq records something else. Today: du'a.

teach.h: A DU'A: A PRAYER IN ONE'S OWN NEED.
teach.b: A du'a is a personal prayer, words addressed to Allah in a person's own need, as opposed to the set prayer, the salah. This one, as Ibn Ishaq gives it, begins with a complaint, but not against Thaqif.
He complains to Allah of his own weakness: his lack of strength, his lack of means, how small he has become in people's eyes. Then he turns.

He calls Allah the most merciful of the merciful, the Lord of the weak, and asks: to whom are You leaving me? To a stranger who will scowl at me, or an enemy given power over me? And then comes today's line.
If You are not angry with me, he says, I don't mind. Your well-being, the ease You give, is wider for me. Look at the order.
First, honesty: I am weak, I have little, people look down on me.

teach.h: TO WHOM ARE YOU LEAVING ME?
teach.b: Then a question, almost a child's: who are You handing me to? Only then the turn, which isn't that the pain stops mattering, but that it's measured against one thing.
If the relationship with Allah is whole, the rest can be borne.
Notice what is missing, too: no curse on Ta'if, no request that the town be punished.

teach.h: IF YOU ARE NOT ANGRY, I DON'T MIND.
teach.b: That restraint will matter in two days. A note on the source: this du'a comes from the sirah, through Ibn Ishaq, not from Bukhari or Muslim, and hadith scholars have discussed the strength of its chain.
Its words are still said today, in hard times.

how: The du'a of Ta'if is taught in sirah study alongside the journey to Ta'if, and Muslims say its words in times of hardship or rejection.

games.q: you're him, alone by an orchard wall after being driven out of a town. you begin to pray. what do you complain of first?
o: the cruelty of the people of Ta'if.
games.why: in Ibn Ishaq's account, the complaint is of his own weakness, lack of means, and lowliness before people.

practice: Sit with your hands open in your lap, and silently name three honest things: where your strength has run low, where you don't have what you need, where you feel small in other people's eyes.

If you pray, you can bring them to Allah in your own words, as plainly as he did, or in the words of the du'a of Ta'if if you know them. If you don't pray, notice what it's like to say them without defending yourself.

wordCard.voice: Du'a, a personal prayer. In an orchard after rejection, he complains to Allah of his own weakness and says: if You are not angry with me, I don't mind. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: calling on Allah; a personal prayer, distinct from the set salah.

carryVoice: Your line: if you're not angry, I don't mind. Honest about weakness, and still turned toward Allah. That's day seven hundred fifty-one.

sources.ref: Ibn Ishaq, Sirat Rasul Allah (the orchard of Utba and Shayba; the du'a: complaint of weakness, 'to whom do You entrust me', 'if You are not angry with me I do not care')
